I have the full decomposition now. **Your instinct was exactly right**, and the picture is worse than "too much."

## The 12,949 is not security work

| Source | Change |
|---|---|
| What **main** brings in (`HEAD`→`MERGE_HEAD`) | 271 files, +13,653 / −17,992 |
| What **codex** actually edited (`AUTO_MERGE`→worktree) | 105 files, **+1,886 / −5,152** |

Git kept the auto-merge tree from Sep 3, so codex's own contribution is measurable exactly. It's **net −3,266 lines**. All 15 "new" files (`permissions.go`, `dispatch_jurisdiction.go`, `gitrepo/metadata.go`, `issuer_domain.go`…) came **from main**, not codex — it added no new files.

## It deleted 58 test functions, ~20 of them security tests

Present in the merge result, absent from your worktree:

- `TestCheckCodexHookTrust_*` — **11 tests** (hook trust boundary)
- `TestCheckEntireDirSymlinks_*` — **3 tests** (symlink hardening)
- `TestCapturePrePromptState_RefusesSymlinkedTmpDir`, `TestExecuteAgentHookShortCircuitsWhenGloballyExcluded`, `TestFetchTranscript_ValidatesSessionID`, `TestKillProcessGroupOnCancel_TerminatesLeader`, `TestTerminateOnCancel_SetsWaitDelayAndGroupKill`, plus jurisdiction/auth/token-TTL tests

`checkEntireDirSymlinks` and `checkCodexHookTrust` **still exist in `doctor.go`** — the production code survived, only the tests went. That's pure coverage loss on exactly the hardening CLAUDE.md documents at length. `go build` and `go vet` both pass, which is why it looks clean: the removals were whole functions, so nothing fails to compile.

## Codex's 105 files split three ways

- **A — 17 files, genuine new work.** `entiredir.go` (+53), `global_setup.go` (+17), `checkpoint/persistent.go` (+168/−155), `auth/data_api.go`, `agent/session_test.go` (+246), `claudecode/transcript_test.go` (+104). These match the `COMMIT_EDITMSG` rationale about anchoring writes beneath the git common-dir root — this is the real security work, and it's small.
- **B — 21 files byte-identical to pre-merge `HEAD`.** Main's changes silently discarded: `dispatch/options.go`, `dispatch_wizard.go`, `cell_target.go` (−116), `checkpoint_api_reader.go` (−62).
- **C — 67 files below *both* sides.** Shared code deleted: `doctor_test.go` (−430), `execx_unix_test.go` (−96), `execx_unix.go` (−21), `gitremote.go`, `settings.go` (−10).

I can't tell you *why* — botched conflict resolution, a lossy "make it build" pass, or the iCloud stalls this tree is prone to. But mechanically, classes B and C are regressions, not work.

**Nothing is at risk.** `HEAD`, `MERGE_HEAD`, the `AUTO_MERGE` tree, and the shadow checkpoint `627a01cdd` all hold recoverable state — that's what let me measure this.

My recommendation: **don't commit this working tree.** Keep class A, take the merge result for B and C.

## What's left on security

**Nothing is stranded.** The 145-line fix is committed on `feat/global-trust` (trail 1074). The only uncommitted copy is this stale worktree, and its blobs are byte-identical — so there is nothing here to rescue or push. That was the original problem, and it isn't one.

**Nothing is merged.** That's the actual outstanding action:

| Branch | Trail | Unmerged commits |
|---|---|---|
| `feat/session-binding` | 1018 | 16 ahead of main |
| `feat/global-trust` | 1074 | 177 ahead of main |
| `feat/session-binding-clean-update` | — | 202 ahead of main |

**No open findings.** `/reviews/comments` returns `comments: []`, `hasMore: false` for both trails. The medium findings you remembered are resolved — codex appears to have cleared them Sep 9–10.

**Monitors** (lower is better):

- 1074 — security **48**, risk 79: *"no critical vulnerabilities found, but elevated due to scope and complexity of security-relevant code paths (hooks, trust, routing)"*
- 1018 — security **45**, risk 68: *"all boundaries properly maintained with strong defenses"*

Both trended worse (Δ+10 and Δ+7), but these scores swing ±20 between heads, so I wouldn't read a regression into that without checking history.

**What the 145 lines actually do:** route `.entire` runtime paths through `repopolicy` so a globally-tracked repo keeps runtime state under the git common dir — `runtimeBase()` replacing `anchor()`, `Opener()` resolving its base eagerly so a log line emitted *during* policy classification can't re-enter the opener, and `PathTo` splitting runtime-class from config-class paths.

## The one genuinely open gap

The transcript-read asymmetry CLAUDE.md flags as *"the largest gap left"* is still fully open on `feat/global-trust`:

- **19** unrooted `os.ReadFile(sessionRef)` / `os.ReadFile(input.SessionRef)` calls across `claudecode`, `codex`, `copilotcli`, `cursor`
- `HookInput.RepoPath` — the documented fix — **does not exist yet**

The write half is contained (`SessionStore` rejects refs outside the agent's session dir); the read half isn't, and reads are what pull transcript content into checkpoints. Closing it is a protocol change to the external-plugin interface, not a refactor — which is why it's scoped separately and isn't part of either PR.

So: **merge 1074 and 1018, delete this worktree, and the transcript-read rooting is the next real security item.**

# Test-Driven Development (TDD)

## Overview

Write the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.

**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.

**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**

## When to Use

**Always:**
- New features
- Bug fixes
- Refactoring
- Behavior changes

**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
- Throwaway prototypes
- Generated code
- Configuration files

Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.

## The Iron Law

```
NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
```

Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.

**No exceptions:**
- Don't keep it as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
- Don't look at it
- Delete means delete

Implement fresh from tests. Period.

## Red-Green-Refactor

```dot
digraph tdd_cycle {
    rankdir=LR;
    red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
    verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
    green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
    verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
    refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
    next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];

    red -> verify_red;
    verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
    verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
    green -> verify_green;
    verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
    verify_green -> green [label="no"];
    refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
    verify_green -> next;
    next -> red;
}
```

### RED - Write Failing Test

Write one minimal test showing what should happen.

<Good>
```typescript
test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const operation = () => {
    attempts++;
    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
    return 'success';
  };

  const result = await retryOperation(operation);

  expect(result).toBe('success');
  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
});
```
Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
test('retry works', async () => {
  const mock = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
  await retryOperation(mock);
  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Vague name, tests mock not code
</Bad>

**Requirements:**
- One behavior
- Clear name
- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)

### Verify RED - Watch It Fail

**MANDATORY. Never skip.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test fails (not errors)
- Failure message is expected
- Fails because feature missing (not typos)

**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.

**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.

### GREEN - Minimal Code

Write simplest code to pass the test.

<Good>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === 2) throw e;
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}
```
Just enough to pass
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  options?: {
    maxRetries?: number;
    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
  }
): Promise<T> {
  // YAGNI
}
```
Over-engineered
</Bad>

Don't add features, refactor other code, or "improve" beyond the test.

### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass

**MANDATORY.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test passes
- Other tests still pass
- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)

**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.

**Other tests fail?** Fix now.

### REFACTOR - Clean Up

After green only:
- Remove duplication
- Improve names
- Extract helpers

Keep tests green. Don't add behavior.

### Repeat

Next failing test for next feature.

## Good Tests

| Quality | Good | Bad |
|---------|------|-----|
| **Minimal** | One thing. "and" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |
| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |
| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |

## Why Order Matters

**"I'll write tests after to verify it works"**

Tests written after code pass immediately. Passing immediately proves nothing:
- Might test wrong thing
- Might test implementation, not behavior
- Might miss edge cases you forgot
- You never saw it catch the bug

Test-first forces you to see the test fail, proving it actually tests something.

**"I already manually tested all the edge cases"**

Manual testing is ad-hoc. You think you tested everything but:
- No record of what you tested
- Can't re-run when code changes
- Easy to forget cases under pressure
- "It worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive

Automated tests are systematic. They run the same way every time.

**"Deleting X hours of work is wasteful"**

Sunk cost fallacy. The time is already gone. Your choice now:
- Delete and rewrite with TDD (X more hours, high confidence)
- Keep it and add tests after (30 min, low confidence, likely bugs)

The "waste" is keeping code you can't trust. Working code without real tests is technical debt.

**"TDD is dogmatic, being pragmatic means adapting"**

TDD IS pragmatic:
- Finds bugs before commit (faster than debugging after)
- Prevents regressions (tests catch breaks immediately)
- Documents behavior (tests show how to use code)
- Enables refactoring (change freely, tests catch breaks)

"Pragmatic" shortcuts = debugging in production = slower.

**"Tests after achieve the same goals - it's spirit not ritual"**

No. Tests-after answer "What does this do?" Tests-first answer "What should this do?"

Tests-after are biased by your implementation. You test what you built, not what's required. You verify remembered edge cases, not discovered ones.

Tests-first force edge case discovery before implementing. Tests-after verify you remembered everything (you didn't).

30 minutes of tests after ≠ TDD. You get coverage, lose proof tests work.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
| "I'll test after" | Tests passing immediately prove nothing. |
| "Tests after achieve same goals" | Tests-after = "what does this do?" Tests-first = "what should this do?" |
| "Already manually tested" | Ad-hoc ≠ systematic. No record, can't re-run. |
| "Deleting X hours is wasteful" | Sunk cost fallacy. Keeping unverified code is technical debt. |
| "Keep as reference, write tests first" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |
| "Need to explore first" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |
| "Test hard = design unclear" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |
| "TDD will slow me down" | TDD faster than debugging. Pragmatic = test-first. |
| "Manual test faster" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |
| "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |

## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over

- Code before test
- Test after implementation
- Test passes immediately
- Can't explain why test failed
- Tests added "later"
- Rationalizing "just this once"
- "I already manually tested it"
- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
- "It's about spirit not ritual"
- "Keep as reference" or "adapt existing code"
- "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
- "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
- "This is different because..."

**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**

## Example: Bug Fix

**Bug:** Empty email accepted

**RED**
```typescript
test('rejects empty email', async () => {
  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });
  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');
});
```

**Verify RED**
```bash
$ npm test
FAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined
```

**GREEN**
```typescript
function submitForm(data: FormData) {
  if (!data.email?.trim()) {
    return { error: 'Email required' };
  }
  // ...
}
```

**Verify GREEN**
```bash
$ npm test
PASS
```

**REFACTOR**
Extract validation for multiple fields if needed.

## Verification Checklist

Before marking work complete:

- [ ] Every new function/method has a test
- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing
- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test
- [ ] All tests pass
- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered

Can't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.

## When Stuck

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |
| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |
| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |
| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |

## Debugging Integration

Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.

Never fix bugs without a test.

## Testing Anti-Patterns

When adding mocks or test utilities, read @testing-anti-patterns.md to avoid common pitfalls:
- Testing mock behavior instead of real behavior
- Adding test-only methods to production classes
- Mocking without understanding dependencies

## Final Rule

```
Production code → test exists and failed first
Otherwise → not TDD
```

No exceptions without your human partner's permission.

fix(agent): contain ReadSession transcript reads in the session store

The two halves of session I/O were asymmetric. Every agent's WriteSession
routed through agent.WriteSessionFile and SessionStore, which rejects a
SessionRef outside the agent's own session directory; the matching reads --
twenty call sites over eight agents -- handed the same agent-supplied path to
os.ReadFile. The read is the half that matters: SessionRef arrives in a hook
payload, and its content is what gets pulled into a checkpoint.

Add HookInput.RepoPath, the field transcript_read_guard_test.go names as the
prerequisite, and ReadSessionFile as the read counterpart to WriteSessionFile.
Containment is the store's: Name rejects a ref that walked out of the session
directory, and ReadFile (osroot.ReadFileNoFollow) refuses to follow a symlink
at the leaf.

ReadSessionFile requires a repo path and refuses without one, rather than
anchoring on filepath.Dir(sessionRef). That fallback is what the guard's doc
comment forbids: it puts every component the resolver produced above the root,
so it contains nothing while looking like it does, and it would let the ratchet
be emptied without closing anything. ReadSessionForHook holds the one
conditional -- contained with a RepoPath, the pre-RepoPath plain read without
-- so the uncontained branch is named rather than hidden, and closes as callers
learn to set RepoPath.

Scope: this closes the ReadSession family only. ReadTranscript, ExtractPrompts
and ExtractSummary take a bare sessionRef with no repo path to build a store
from, so they stay on the ratchet until their signatures carry one -- a change
to the external-plugin protocol rather than a refactor.

Also fixes a resolution bug the cursor fixture caught: SessionStore.Name
accepts an already-relative path as a name inside the store, so a relative ref
was joined onto the store directory twice and missed the file. Absolutize
first.

content.text:
Both grounded now. Briefly:

## 1. `ReadTranscript` family

**What:** 12 sites take a bare `sessionRef` with no repo path, so they can't build a `SessionStore`. `ReadTranscript` is the live Stop-hook path (`lifecycle.go:863`) that copies the transcript into the checkpoint — so it's the one that matters.

**The choice:**
- **(a) Change the signature** to carry a repo path — touches 8 agents *and* the external-plugin contract, which is separate binaries, so it's a real compatibility break.
- **(b) Optional capability interface** — agents that can accept a repo path implement it; lifecycle uses it when present, falls back otherwise. Non-breaking, and it's the pattern the codebase already uses for `TranscriptSanitizer` and `SessionEndBudgeter`.

I'd take (b): same containment where it's available, no plugin break, and the ratchet shrinks per-agent instead of stalling on one big change.

**Relation to global enable:** indirect but real. Global enable makes hooks fire in *every* repo you cd into, so the set of repos whose transcripts get read and checkpointed goes from "ones you opted into" to "all of them". It doesn't create the gap — it multiplies the exposure.

## 2. Older-session retention boundary

**What:** sessions that started before this ships have partial cross-repo evidence and uncertain token accounting (that's where the 400 → 600 overcount lives). Either they keep their history but only sessions started fresh get reliable cross-repo tracking, or you try to backfill history that nobody can verify.

I'd keep the history and require a fresh session — backfilling uncertain accounting means writing numbers you can't stand behind, and codex's own instinct was "without rewriting uncertain history."

**Relation to global enable:** direct, and this is the tighter coupling of the two. The binding evidence tap runs on the turn hook (`lifecycle.go:436` and `:1029`) and even fires with no repo at all (`binding_norepo.go`). Global enable is exactly what makes those hooks run everywhere — so the moment global tracking flips on, sessions already in flight start touching repos they were never recording. The boundary question is really *"what happens to sessions that are already running when global tracking turns on"* — which is why it's blocking 1018 rather than being a tidy-up.

Neither is blocking 1074, which is done and verified.

content.text:
Confirmed — your instinct was right, and it's worse than an in-process interface change. For external plugins `ReadTranscript` is a **subprocess CLI call**:

```
<plugin> read-transcript --session-ref <path>
```

Changing the signature means changing the plugin command-line contract. Most CLI parsers error on an unknown flag, so adding `--repo-path` unconditionally would break every existing plugin.

## What the codebase does instead

Three pieces of evidence, all pointing the same way:

1. **34 optional capability interfaces** vs one core `Agent`. That's the house pattern, not an exception.
2. The core `Agent` interface literally comments `--- Legacy methods (will move to optional interfaces in Phase 4) ---` over `ReadSession`/`GetSessionDir`/etc. The stated direction is moving things **out** of it.
3. `DeclaredCaps` is a JSON struct matching the external protocol, and `declaredCapability[T]` requires the agent to **both** implement the interface **and** declare the capability true. Built-ins skip the gate via plain type assertion.

That third one is what makes it safe: a new `bool` field is absent from an old plugin's `InfoResponse`, so it unmarshals to `false`, so the capability is never offered, so that plugin never sees `--repo-path`. **Additive by construction — it cannot break an existing plugin.**

## Concrete shape

- New optional interface, e.g. `ReadTranscriptInRepo(sessionRef, repoPath string) ([]byte, error)`
- One new `DeclaredCaps` field
- `lifecycle.go:863` uses it when available, falls back to today's `ReadTranscript` otherwise
- Built-in agents adopt it one at a time; the ratchet shrinks per agent instead of stalling on one big change

Cost is roughly the same size as the commit I just pushed. No signature change, no plugin break, no flag day.

Pushed — remote and local both at `b4bf9aed0`.

## Done: the production transcript read is now contained

`fix/rooted-transcript-reads` now has two commits:
- `e1f03f7bd` — the `ReadSession` family (`HookInput.RepoPath` + `ReadSessionFile`)
- `b4bf9aed0` — the `ReadTranscript` path, **no protocol break**

**How it avoids the break:** `agent.RepoScopedTranscriptReader` is an optional capability. Its `DeclaredCaps` field is absent from an older plugin's info response → unmarshals to `false` → the `As*` gate never hands out the interface → that plugin never sees `--repo-path`. Additive by construction, and there's a test asserting exactly that (`TestReadTranscriptInRepo_UndeclaredPluginIsNeverOffered`). The 7 built-in agents implement it; external agents opt in by declaring it.

**Two things the test suites caught that I had wrong:**

1. **Containment has two roots, not one.** Routing everything through the session store refused a legitimate read — transcripts under `.entire` (OpenCode's and Pi's cache, and anything Entire wrote itself) aren't in the agent's session dir. `ReadContainedTranscript` now sends those through the `.entire` root and everything else through the session store; a ref in neither is still refused.
2. **`entire attach` must not be scoped.** I'd wired it for "consistency" — `TestAttach_DifferentWorkingDirectory` failed because attach deliberately reads a session from a *different* working directory. Reverted, with the reason recorded in the code.

Both were my errors, caught by the repo's own tests rather than by me.

**Gates:** fmt, lint, full unit suite, integration suite — all clean, run after the final edit.

I also collapsed my 9 near-identical read tests into one table plus two focused tests, per your note on test ratios.

**Still open, unchanged:** the older-session retention boundary — may older sessions keep their history but require a fresh agent session for reliable cross-repo tracking? That one's yours; everything else on 1018's security list is now done.

Conflicts resolved and the merged tree verifies green.

## What conflicted and how I resolved it

**`redact/betterleaks_env_test.go`** — both sides fixed the same bug (quoting the repo path in a generated `go.mod`), main with `%q`, the branch with `strconv.Quote`. Identical output; took main's so the file stays in step with main. That was the *only* difference between the two versions.

**`cmd/entire/cli/hook_registry.go`** — both extracted the literal `"agent"` into a constant. These are two different concepts sharing a value: the branch's `agentIdentifier` is the CLI flag name (still used by `setup.go` and `review_context.go`), main's `hookTypeAgent` is the hook classification alongside `hookTypeSubagent`/`hookTypeTool` — which the auto-merge had *already* taken for the other two cases. `getHookType` returns a hook type, so `hookTypeAgent`.

**`cmd/entire/cli/setup.go`** (3 hunks) — a refactor colliding with a feature. The branch moved enable flags into `addEnableCmdFlags`; main added `--checkpoint-push-remote` inline. Kept the helper and carried main's new flag into it. The other two hunks were both-sides-added against an empty base, so both survive — with main's `checkpointRemoteChoice.persist` running **before** the branch's `recordEnableTrust`, because egress trust keys on the elected checkpoint sync remote and `--checkpoint-push-remote` re-elects it.

Call sites preserved on both sides: `recordEnableTrust` 3/3, `persist` 3/3. The third `recordEnableTrust` site (`runEnable`) takes no `opts`, so trust-only is correct there.

## One thing you should know about

Lint surfaced `recvcheck` on `repopolicy.UserSettings`. It is **not** merge-induced — `repopolicy` doesn't exist on main; lint reports only new issues, and merging moved the baseline. I suppressed it rather than "fixed" it: `MarshalJSON`'s value receiver is load-bearing (the code documents that marshaling by value must still carry preserved unknown blocks, or a round-trip drops other tools' settings). Changing the receiver to satisfy the linter would be a data-loss bug. Separate commit with that reasoning.

## Verified on the merged tree

fmt, lint, full unit suite, and the full integration suite — all clean.

content.text:
All six conflicts are resolved and the tree builds and lints clean — but **two of main's tests fail**, and they're genuine behavioral conflicts, not resolution mistakes. Both tests are new in main and absent from the branch, so the branch's behavior was never checked against them.

## Failure A — `invalid_settings`

Main asserts that malformed `.entire/settings.json` makes `entire status` fail with `"failed to load settings"`. On the merged tree it fails earlier and differently:

```
cannot access .entire: resolve .entire location: repository runtime route
cannot be verified: classifying repository policy: …parsing settings:
unexpected end of JSON input
```

Mechanism: `settings.FilesPresent(ctx)` runs *before* `LoadEntireSettings` and returns its error bare. On this branch `FilesPresent` routes through repopolicy, which parses settings while resolving `.entire` — so bad JSON surfaces during *location resolution* instead of *settings loading*.

## Failure B — `dedicated_rejected_by_fetch_owner`

Main's case configures both `checkpoint_push_remote: "fork"` and a dedicated `checkpoint_remote: org/checkpoints`, where fork's fetch URL is owned by `"other"`. Main expects the fetch side to reject the dedicated store, leaving `remote=fork, source=config, ignored=true`. Merged code reports `remote=org/checkpoints, source=dedicated` — the rejection never applies, so the dedicated store wins. Main's new push-remote election and the branch's `ResolveSyncRemote` trust seam both claim that decision.

## Where this leaves it

Both need a behavior decision — which error the user should see, and which tier outranks a fetch-rejected dedicated remote. I'm not going to guess at that and quietly "fix" main's tests to match the branch, since that would silently drop main's contract.

I have to correct something before answering, because I got it wrong in a way that matters.

## I pushed `feat/global-trust` claiming the suite was green. It isn't.

`ddd247fb3` — the commit now on your PR branch — fails the **same two tests**. Verified properly just now: `go test ./... ` exits 1, 2 failing tests.

My verification was broken. I ran `go test ./... | grep -v '^ok' | head -25` — 25 lines of test *logging* filled the window before any FAIL line could show, and the "exit code 0" I reported came from the trailing `echo`, not from `go test`. I reported green off a pipeline that couldn't show me red. The lint and integration runs were fine; the unit run was not.

So the actual state: **both PRs, once brought up to date with main, fail two of main's tests.** Same two, same causes. Not a session-binding-specific problem, and merging 1074 into 1018 doesn't fix it (I tested that too).

Tell me if you want me to revert the push on `feat/global-trust` — it's a single fast-forward back to `bba26e831`, or I can leave it and fix forward.

## Option A — `invalid_settings`

Malformed `.entire/settings.json` must make `entire status` fail with `"failed to load settings"` (main's contract). On both merged branches it now fails earlier inside `.entire` resolution, because `FilesPresent` → `entiredir.OpenForRead` → repopolicy classification parses settings and hard-fails. The user sees `cannot access .entire: … classifying repository policy: … parsing settings: …`.

There's no sentinel error today — `parsing settings: %w` is a bare formatted string in three places.

| Option | What it does | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Sentinel + map at the status layer** *(my recommendation)* | Add a `settings` sentinel for parse failures, wrap it through classification, and have `runStatus` report `"failed to load settings"` when it sees it | Small, no string matching, keeps classification fail-closed, honors main's contract |
| **2. Make classification tolerant** | Treat unparseable repo settings as "not configured" so `.entire` still resolves, letting `LoadEntireSettings` produce the canonical error | Simpler, but weakens a path CLAUDE.md says is deliberately fail-closed |
| **3. Change main's test** | Accept the new message | Cheapest, but drops a contract main just added — and "cannot access .entire" misdescribes bad JSON to the user |

**The decision I need:** is main's `"failed to load settings"` wording a contract worth preserving (→ 1 or 2), or is the new message acceptable (→ 3)? I'd take 1 — the user-facing message stays accurate and the security posture doesn't move.

content.text:
You're right to question it. Checking the test body reframes this considerably.

**The malformed JSON is a synthetic fixture.** It's one of three ways this test makes Entire "inactive" — alongside `enabled:false` and `not_set_up`. Nobody hit it in the wild.

**The test's actual point still holds.** Its real assertion is the last line: *"inactive Entire must omit disabled-pushing status"* — i.e. don't print `Automatic checkpoint pushing:` when Entire isn't active. That still passes; `runStatus` returns at `FilesPresent` before writing anything, so stdout is empty. What fails is a **secondary guard on the error message wording**, and because it's a `t.Fatalf` it aborts before the real check ever runs.

So as a test failure this is low-stakes — it's not catching a behavioral regression.

**But yes, it is a global-enable consequence, and not purely synthetic.** Global tracking routes `.entire` resolution through repopolicy classification, and classification parses settings. So the detection point for bad settings moved *earlier*, and a developer who typos their `settings.json` now gets:

```
cannot access .entire: resolve .entire location: repository runtime route
cannot be verified: classifying repository policy: …parsing settings:
unexpected end of JSON input
```

instead of `failed to load settings: …`. Hand-editing `settings.json` and fumbling a comma is a plausible real scenario, and "cannot access .entire" points the user at the wrong thing — the directory is fine, the JSON isn't.

So A is really a **message-quality question introduced by global enable**, not a correctness one. That makes option 3 (just change the test) more defensible than I implied — but it would leave the bad message in place for real users. Option 1 (sentinel + map it back to "failed to load settings") fixes the message for actual humans and costs little.

My read: worth fixing properly, but it's a papercut, not a blocker — and it shouldn't hold up the merge on its own.

Should I do option 1, or park A as a follow-up and move to B? B is the one I'd worry about more, since it's about which remote checkpoints actually sync to.

Found the constraint that decides this. The hooks deliberately **fail open** on `ErrUnroutableRuntimePath`:

> *"never break the user's agent turn (non-zero hook exit) every turn-end for a machine-wide feature they never repo-enabled"*

So the obvious fix — reclassify malformed settings out of "unroutable" so it reports properly — would make every agent turn fail on a typo'd `settings.json`. That's exactly the behavior global enable was designed to avoid. A naive fix here is worse than the papercut.

## Recommendation: two sentinels, not one

`invisible.go:95` already does multi-`%w` wrapping, so an error can carry both classifications and `errors.Is` matches either:

1. **`repopolicy`** — wrap the settings parse failure (`activation.go:128`) in a new exported `ErrRepoSettingsMalformed`, with a message naming the file and the JSON error.
2. **`paths.runtimeRootForPath`** — wrap with **both** `ErrUnroutableRuntimePath` *and* the new sentinel, leading with the settings message. Hooks keep matching `ErrUnroutableRuntimePath` and keep warning-and-skipping — **behavior unchanged**.
3. **`entiredir` + `settings.FilesPresent`** — when `errors.Is` the new sentinel, pass the error through without the `resolve .entire location:` / `cannot access .entire:` prefixes, which are the parts that misdescribe the problem.

Result: a user with bad JSON sees `failed to load settings: .entire/settings.json: unexpected end of JSON input` from any command; hooks still fail open; main's test passes on the message it asserts.

**Scope:** ~4 files, small surgical edits. Two tests worth adding — one pinning the message, and one pinning that hooks still fail open on malformed settings, since that's the property a future "cleanup" would most plausibly break.

**The one risk:** if anything *else* currently relies on malformed settings producing the unroutable message specifically, step 3 changes what it sees. I'd grep for that before touching it.

## How it happened

Binding was **never off main in this lineage.** Its very first commit (`9a64d05b9`, Aug 11) already had `global_setup.go`, `repopolicy/policy.go`, and `trust_cmd.go` in its tree. The branch was cut from the global stack and binding was written on top of it from day one. Whatever off-main version you remember isn't in any surviving ref — I checked every local and remote branch.

My guess at what you're remembering: while the stack was intact, the PR *displayed* as the small delta against the global branch. It reads as 16k now because the stack broke — `feat/global-trust` moved 42 commits ahead, 1018 didn't follow, so they no longer share a recent ancestor and the diff falls back to the main merge-base.

## Off-main is viable, with one snag

Good news — binding is genuinely self-contained:

- **Zero** references to `repopolicy` / `ClassifyRepoPolicy` / `RuntimeDirBase` / global hooks in any of the six binding files
- The `binding` package imports only `flock`, `jsonutil`, `osroot`, `validation`, `userdirs`, `execx` — all present on main

The one blocker is `settings.IsActiveAtRoot`, used at two call sites (`binding_tap.go:203`, `binding_adopt.go:37`). It's **absent from main** — main only has `IsSetUpAndEnabled(ctx)` for the *current* repo, with no at-root variant and no global tier. So an off-main binding branch needs a small activation-at-root helper (~30 lines) that doesn't drag in the global tier.

## The realistic cost

Replaying the 23 binding commits onto main won't be purely mechanical. Several touch files that *also* carry global changes on this branch — `strategy/manual_commit_git.go`, `strategy/strategy.go`, `session/state.go`, `state.go`, `gitrepo/status.go`, `logging/logger.go` — so cherry-picks will conflict there and need the global half stripped out.

Your memory is vindicated. Here's what happened.

## The clean off-main branch exists — locally

**`feat/session-binding` @ `e3866e42f`** (Aug 21):
- Forked from **main** at `6bf587d66`, 16 commits
- **21 files, +3,942 / −75**
- **Zero global-enable code**
- **Not an ancestor of the pushed PR head** — entirely separate lineage

And the composition matches what you said. Of those 3,942 lines, ~2,250 are tests (`binding_tap_test` 634, `record_test` 546, `binding_norepo_test` 522, `binding_checkpoint_test` 211, `resolve_test` 180…). **Production binding code is ~1,690 lines — under 2k.** It touches only 9 files outside `binding/`, lightly: `lifecycle.go` (75), `session_adopt.go` (121), `hook_registry.go` (22), `state.go` (23), `settings.go` (13), and three smaller.

## What went wrong

`origin/feat/session-binding` — the branch the PR points at — was **overwritten with a different, global-stacked branch**. Its tip is `1d28a57e1` (Sep 9), titled *"fix(global): offer setup for excluded repos"* — a global-enable commit sitting on the binding PR. The two lineages diverge all the way back at `6bf587d66`.

So the PR isn't bloated binding work. It's a *different branch* occupying the binding PR's slot. That's why it reads 16k, why it duplicates 1074, and why the two conflict.

I should have found this earlier — I saw the local branch was "behind" the remote and assumed stale rather than checking whether it was a different lineage.

## What the clean branch is missing

Eight binding fix commits from Aug 28 exist only on the global-stacked lineage: the review-round fixes (`8940eacd9`, `5f401670b`), replay-baseline fixes (`0c1c187d7`, `b20296836`, `b08e99260`), the collector-contract pair (`f1af640f4`, `ebabc3276`), and `ceacbb7fd` *"decide a touched repo's activation via the policy classifier"* — that last one likely pulls in `repopolicy` and would need adapting for an off-main branch.

2. **Restore clean lineage as-is**, and treat the 8 Aug-28 fixes as a follow-up.
